thread.title: Fewer corporate giants face tax audits

author: Anthony Noto
title: Fewer corporate giants face tax audits
text: – Reporter, New York Business Journal Apr 11, 2018, 10:49am EDT With tax day approaching on April 17, it's worth noting that if you miss the deadline, the odds of receiving an audit from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) are low. Recent statistics show less than 1 percent of American individuals get audited by the IRS and only about 15 percent of Americans with annual incomes of $10 million or more get audited. Also, less than 1 percent of small businesses get audited. For so-called "corporate giants" — those with more than $20 billion in assets — there's still a very good chance, a bit more than 50-50, that they could get audited. However, the number of audits of these super-sized companies has dropped significantly over the last eight years. According to a new report from Syracuse University , during the fiscal year of 2017, the government agency audited just over half, 54 percent (331), of these large companies. The IRS reports that nationally there are now 616 corporate giants — a number that has grown by more than a third (38 percent) over the past seven years. The number of IRS audits of these mammoth companies has not grown. According to the data, compiled by the school's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), audits have been falling (see infographic above). As recently as fiscal year 2010, 96 percent of corporate giant received an IRS audit. By 2016, this had fallen to only three out of four, or 76 percent. And in 2017, nearly half of these corporate behemoths escaped any IRS audit. Congressional cutbacks to IRS's budget is most likely the reason why there are fewer audits, TRAC concluded. This has led to staff cuts, meaning the number of available IRS revenue agents — those who examine corporate and high income individual returns — has decreased. Basically, fewer auditors mean that fewer audits can be conducted at a time when the tax arrangements of companies like Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL), Microsoft and Amazon.com have drawn increasing scrutiny. Last year, there were 5,144 fewer IRS revenue agents employed than there had been in FY 2010. Over the past seven years, revenue agents have fallen by over a third (34.9 percent). Also an issue are the sweeping changes to the tax laws that go into effect for 2018. Passage of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), signed by President Donald Trump on Dec. 22, comes with new responsibilities and demands on the IRS: "Without adequate resources to meet already existing needs, IRS's efforts to meet these new demands can only exacerbate existing problems," the report continued. "The prognosis for the future and for the health of our federal income tax system appears hardly reassuring." Still, it's worth noting that the odds of any American getting picked for an audit is low each year, but there's almost a 100 percent chance they'll get the call every other year. – Reporter, New York Business Journal Apr 11, 2018, 10:49am EDT Related Content
